title: What Happens When We Die? Why Is There Suffering?
bigQuestion: How do the world's traditions explain death and suffering, and how do their answers shape the way people grieve?

story.title: After the Funeral
story.kicker: Four cousins leave their grandmother's funeral with the same loss and four different sets of words for it.
paragraphs: The funeral Mass for Grandma Rosa was held at a parish on Chicago's Southwest Side, the church where she had been baptized, married and, for sixty years, a Sunday regular. The priest spoke of the resurrection and of a life that had not ended but changed. Her rosary was placed in her hands in the casket. Afterward the family drove to the cemetery, and then everyone crowded into her small brick house, where the neighbors had already covered the kitchen table with food.

The four oldest cousins ended up on the back porch. Daniela, who still went to Mass with her parents, said she was sure Grandma was with God. Noah, whose father is Jewish, said his dad's family would be sitting shiva for a week if this were their funeral, with the mirrors covered and people bringing meals. He was not sure what his father's side believed happened after death, and he realized he had never asked.

Anjali's mother is Hindu, and Anjali had been to her grandfather's cremation in India two summers before. She remembered the priest, the fire and the ashes carried to the river. Her mother had told her that the soul does not die, that it moves on to another life the way a person changes clothes. Sam, who had grown up with no religion, said quietly that he thought Grandma was simply gone. What he could not stop thinking about was the last two years, when she had been in pain almost every day.

That was the question that silenced them. Why had someone so kind suffered so long? Daniela said Grandma had offered her pain to God and kept her rosary in the hospital. Anjali said her mother would talk about karma, though not as a punishment. Noah remembered a rabbi at his cousin's bar mitzvah saying that the Book of Job was written for exactly this question and never fully answers it. Sam said maybe there was no reason at all.

Nobody won the argument, and nobody tried to. Late in the evening an aunt came out with plates of cake and said that Grandma would have liked seeing them talk. The cousins had just done, without a textbook, what this chapter asks you to do: put the answers side by side, attribute each to its tradition, and notice where they meet and where they part.
story.think: Each cousin reached for words from a tradition, or from none. Why might the words a family uses at a death matter so much to the people left behind?

lessons.title: Judaism: This World and the World to Come
lessons.mainIdea: The Hebrew Bible focuses on life in this world, while later Jewish tradition taught resurrection and the world to come, and Jewish movements still differ on how to understand them.
reading: Most of the Hebrew Bible says little about life after death. The dead go down to *Sheol*, a shadowy place of silence, and the Psalms ask whether the dead can praise God at all. The Torah's promises of blessing and punishment concern this life: long days in the land, children, harvests. For much of ancient Israel, a person lived on through descendants, through the people and through a good name.

Near the end of the biblical period the picture changes. The Book of Daniel, which most scholars date to the second century BCE, contains the Hebrew Bible's clearest statement of *resurrection*, the dead rising to life again, quoted below. By the first century CE Jews disagreed about it. The Pharisees taught resurrection. The Sadducees, the priestly party, rejected it because they found it nowhere in the Torah. The rabbis who shaped later Judaism followed the Pharisees.

Rabbinic tradition speaks of *Olam Ha-Ba*, the world to come, where the righteous receive their reward. Maimonides, the great twelfth-century scholar, included resurrection of the dead among his Thirteen Principles of Faith. The traditional daily prayer praises God, who gives life to the dead. Many rabbinic sources describe Gehinnom as a place of purification rather than endless punishment, often lasting no more than twelve months.

Modern movements read these teachings differently. Orthodox Jews generally affirm bodily resurrection. Classical Reform Judaism, in its 1885 Pittsburgh Platform, set bodily resurrection aside in favor of the immortality of the soul, and many Reform and Reconstructionist Jews today speak more of memory, legacy and the soul than of a future rising. Across all of them, Jewish teaching tends to keep the emphasis on this life: on keeping the commandments now, not on speculating about what comes after.

words.d: in the Hebrew Bible, the shadowy place of the dead, where all go after death
the dead being raised to life again, in body, at the end of time
Hebrew for the world to come; in rabbinic Judaism, the life or age of reward after this one

look.title: Those Who Sleep in the Dust
look.text: And many of them that sleep in the dust of the earth shall awake, some to everlasting life, and some to shame and everlasting contempt.
look.prompt: The verse calls death sleep and resurrection waking. What does that image suggest about how its author thought of death? Why might a verse like this matter to Jews living under persecution, as most scholars think Daniel's first readers were?

check.q: How does most of the Hebrew Bible describe the place of the dead?
choices: As Sheol, a shadowy place of silence
As a paradise garden for the righteous
As a cycle of rebirth into new bodies
As a place of fire for all sinners
check.why: Most of the Hebrew Bible speaks of Sheol, a dim place of the dead, and places reward and punishment in this life.

check.q: Why did the Sadducees reject resurrection?
choices: Because Maimonides had rejected it
Because they found it nowhere in the Torah
Because they believed in rebirth instead
Because the Pharisees had banned it
check.why: The Sadducees, the priestly party, accepted only what they found in the Torah, and they did not find resurrection there.

check.q: What did the Reform movement's 1885 Pittsburgh Platform do with bodily resurrection?
choices: It made it the center of Jewish belief
It required all Reform Jews to affirm it daily
It set it aside in favor of the immortality of the soul
It moved it from the Talmud into the Torah
check.why: Classical Reform Judaism, in the Pittsburgh Platform, set aside bodily resurrection and spoke instead of the soul's immortality.

lessons.title: Christianity: The Empty Tomb
lessons.mainIdea: Christians believe that Jesus rose from the dead and that his resurrection promises the resurrection of all, followed by judgment and eternal life, though churches differ on the details.
reading: One of the earliest Christian writings on death is a letter. Around 55 CE Paul wrote to the church in Corinth, where some doubted that the dead would rise. His answer, in 1 Corinthians 15, is that everything depends on one event. If Christ has not been raised, he writes, the faith is empty. Christians believe that Jesus was crucified, buried and raised on the third day, and they celebrate that event each year at *Easter*.

For Christians, Jesus's resurrection is the first of many. Paul calls Christ the firstfruits of those who have died, and he describes a resurrection body that is transformed, no longer subject to decay. The Nicene Creed, recited in many churches every Sunday, ends by looking for the resurrection of the dead and the life of the world to come. Christians teach a final *judgment*, pictured in Matthew 25, where the nations are judged by how they treated the hungry, the stranger and the prisoner.

Most Christians believe that at death the soul goes to God, awaiting the final resurrection. Heaven is described as life in God's presence and hell as separation from God. Branches differ here. Roman Catholic teaching includes *purgatory*, a state of purification for those who die in God's grace but not yet fully cleansed. Catholics pray for the dead for that reason. Protestant churches rejected purgatory at the Reformation, and Orthodox Christians pray for the dead without defining purgatory as Catholics do.

Christians also differ on who will be saved and on how literally to take the images of fire and gold streets. Some hold that only those who explicitly trust in Christ are saved. Others hope that God's mercy may reach further. What they share is the conviction, stated in the Gospel of John and quoted below, that death is not the last word because of what they believe happened on Easter morning.

words.d: the Christian festival celebrating the resurrection of Jesus from the dead
in Christian, Jewish and Muslim teaching, God's final assessment of each person's life
in Roman Catholic teaching, a state of purification after death for those who die in God's grace

look.title: I Am the Resurrection
look.text: Jesus said unto her, I am the resurrection, and the life: he that believeth in me, though he were dead, yet shall he live:
look.prompt: Jesus says this to Martha before raising her brother Lazarus. Compare it with Daniel 12:2. Where does each text place the hope of resurrection: in an event at the end of time, in a person, or in both?

check.q: According to Paul in 1 Corinthians 15, what does Christian faith depend on?
choices: The building of the Temple
The Ten Commandments
Good deeds outweighing bad ones
The resurrection of Christ
check.why: Paul writes that if Christ has not been raised, the faith is empty; the resurrection is the event everything rests on.

check.q: In Matthew 25, by what are the nations judged?
choices: By how they treated the hungry, the stranger and the prisoner
By how many prayers they said
By which language they spoke
By whether they kept the Sabbath
check.why: In Matthew 25 the nations are judged by their care for the hungry, the stranger and the prisoner.

check.q: Which Christian branch teaches purgatory as a defined state of purification?
choices: Protestant churches
Roman Catholic teaching
All Christian churches equally
No Christian church
check.why: Purgatory is Roman Catholic teaching; Protestants rejected it at the Reformation, and the Orthodox do not define it the same way.

lessons.title: Islam: The Day of Judgment
lessons.mainIdea: Muslims believe that after death each soul waits in the barzakh until the Day of Judgment, when all are raised, their deeds weighed, and they enter paradise or hell.
reading: When a Muslim dies, the body is washed, wrapped in plain white cloth and buried quickly, usually within a day, facing Mecca. Muslims do not cremate. The plain shroud is the same for rich and poor. It expresses a belief the Qur'an repeats on nearly every page: every person will return to God and give an account. Belief in the Last Day is one of the six articles of faith that Sunni Muslims list, alongside belief in God, angels, scriptures, prophets and God's decree.

The Qur'an calls the life to come *akhira*, the hereafter, and sets it against dunya, this present world. Between death and the end, according to Islamic teaching, the soul waits in the *barzakh*, a barrier or interval. Then comes the Day of Resurrection. The Qur'an describes the earth shaking and giving up its dead, the sky splitting, and every person raised in body to face judgment. Early suras of Mecca describe these scenes in vivid, rhythmic language.

On that day, according to the Qur'an, deeds are weighed on a scale, and each person receives a record of what they did. Sura 99, one of the shortest, says that whoever has done an atom's weight of good will see it, and whoever has done an atom's weight of evil will see it. The righteous enter *jannah*, the garden, described with rivers, shade and peace. The wicked enter jahannam, the fire. The Qur'an stresses throughout that God is merciful and that no soul bears another's burden.

Muslims differ on some details. Scholars have debated whether punishment in jahannam is eternal for all who enter it, and many hold that believers who sinned may be purified and then brought out by God's mercy. Sufi writers often dwell on the soul's longing to meet God more than on the scales. Shia and Sunni Muslims share the core teaching on resurrection and judgment. What stands out in comparison is how closely Islam ties the hereafter to daily life: each prayer, each gift of zakat, each act of honesty is recorded.

words.d: Arabic for the hereafter, the life after death that the Qur'an sets against this present world
in Islamic teaching, the interval in which the soul waits between death and the Day of Resurrection
Arabic for the garden; paradise in the Qur'an

look.title: An Atom's Weight
look.text: In its own words, a short sura describes the earth shaking violently and giving up its burdens, and people asking what has happened to it. On that day people come forward in groups to be shown their deeds. Anyone who has done good the weight of the smallest particle will see it, and anyone who has done evil the weight of the smallest particle will see it.
look.cite: Qur'an, Sura 99 (al-Zalzala, The Earthquake), paraphrased; compare Rodwell (1861) and Palmer (1880)
look.prompt: The sura says even the smallest deed will be seen. How might that belief shape the way a Muslim thinks about an ordinary afternoon? Compare it with Matthew 25.

check.q: How is a Muslim body usually prepared and buried?
choices: Cremated, with ashes placed in a river
Kept at home for forty days
Washed, wrapped in a plain white cloth and buried quickly facing Mecca
Placed in a family tomb above ground with jewels
check.why: Muslims wash and shroud the body in plain cloth and bury it quickly facing Mecca; Islam does not permit cremation.

check.q: What is the barzakh in Islamic teaching?
choices: The scale on which deeds are weighed
The garden of paradise
The final fire
The interval in which the soul waits between death and resurrection
check.why: The barzakh, meaning barrier or interval, is where the soul waits between death and the Day of Resurrection.

check.q: What does Sura 99 teach about deeds?
choices: Even an atom's weight of good or evil will be seen on the Day
Only very great deeds are remembered
Deeds do not matter if one says the right words
Deeds are erased at death
check.why: Sura 99 says that anyone who has done an atom's weight of good or evil will see it on the Day of Judgment.

lessons.title: Hinduism: The Soul Changes Clothes
lessons.mainIdea: Many Hindus believe the atman passes through many lives in samsara, shaped by karma, until it reaches moksha, release from rebirth.
reading: At the burning ghats of Varanasi, on the banks of the Ganges, cremation fires burn day and night. Many Hindus hope to die in Varanasi or to have their ashes placed in the Ganges, a river they regard as holy. A Hindu funeral, *antyesti*, usually ends in cremation, often lit by the eldest son. Rites for the dead continue for about ten to thirteen days, varying by region and community, and families later offer food and prayers for their ancestors in rites called shraddha.

The belief behind the fire is that the body dies but the self does not. Hindu texts call the true self the *atman*. In the Bhagavad Gita, Krishna tells Arjuna that the self is never born and never dies, and that it casts off worn-out bodies as a person casts off worn-out clothes, as shown below. The atman moves through *samsara*, the cycle of birth, death and rebirth, taking many forms across many lives.

What shapes each new life is karma, the principle that actions have consequences that follow a person, in this life and the next. Good actions lead to better births; harmful ones to harder births. Karma in this sense is not a judge's sentence. Hindu teachers describe it more like a law of nature, the way a seed produces its own kind of plant. It explains, in this view, why lives begin in such different circumstances.

The goal is not endless rebirth but release from it, called *moksha*. Hindu paths describe moksha differently. For the Advaita Vedanta school, it is realizing that atman is Brahman, the one ultimate reality, like a drop recognizing it is the ocean. For many devotional traditions, devoted to Vishnu, Krishna or Shiva, it is an eternal life of love in God's presence. Both views agree that death is a passage, not an end, and that how one lives now shapes where the passage leads.

words.d: in Hindu thought, the true, eternal self or soul
the cycle of birth, death and rebirth taught in Hindu, Buddhist, Jain and Sikh traditions
in Hindu thought, liberation from the cycle of rebirth
the Hindu funeral rite, the last sacrifice, usually ending in cremation

look.title: Worn-Out Clothes
look.text: Krishna tells Arjuna that just as a person throws away worn-out garments and puts on new ones, so the embodied self throws away worn-out bodies and enters new ones. Weapons cannot cut it, fire cannot burn it, water cannot wet it and wind cannot dry it. It is eternal and unchanging.
look.cite: Bhagavad Gita 2.22–24, paraphrased; compare Edwin Arnold, The Song Celestial (1885)
look.prompt: Krishna uses this image to comfort a warrior afraid of killing his relatives. Why might the same image comfort a grieving family at a cremation? What does the image assume about what a person really is?

check.q: What happens to the atman at death, according to many Hindus?
choices: It ends forever with the body
It sleeps in Sheol until the end of time
It is weighed on a scale and sent to the garden
It passes on to a new body, as a person changes clothes
check.why: The Gita teaches that the atman casts off worn-out bodies and takes new ones, moving through samsara.

check.q: How do Hindu teachers usually describe karma?
choices: As a law of consequences, like a seed producing its own plant
As a judge's sentence handed down after death
As a prayer said at funerals
As the name of the river at Varanasi
check.why: Karma is described as a natural law of consequences, not a judge's verdict.

check.q: How does Advaita Vedanta describe moksha?
choices: As rebirth into a royal family
As realizing that atman is Brahman, like a drop knowing it is the ocean
As waiting in the barzakh
As the resurrection of the body
check.why: Advaita Vedanta teaches that liberation is realizing the self's identity with Brahman, the one ultimate reality.

lessons.title: Buddhism: Rebirth Without a Soul
lessons.mainIdea: Buddhists teach rebirth driven by karma but deny a permanent self that passes from life to life, and the goal is nirvana, the ending of the cycle.
reading: Buddhists share the picture of samsara with their Hindu neighbors, but with a striking change. The Buddha taught *anatta*, non-self: there is no permanent, unchanging soul inside a person. What we call a self is a changing stream of body, feelings, perceptions, mental formations and consciousness. So what is reborn? A Buddhist text called the Questions of King Milinda answers with an image of a lamp lit from another lamp. The flame is neither the same flame nor a different one.

What carries over, Buddhists teach, is the momentum of karma, intentional action and its results. A life shaped by craving, hatred and delusion tends toward rebirth in painful conditions; a life shaped by generosity, kindness and wisdom toward better ones. Traditional Buddhist cosmology describes several realms of rebirth, including humans, animals, hungry ghosts, hell beings and gods. None of them is permanent, and even the heavens eventually end.

The goal is to stop the cycle altogether. *Nirvana* means blowing out, as a flame goes out when its fuel is gone. The fuel, in Buddhist teaching, is craving. A person who reaches nirvana is not reborn at death. The Buddha declined to describe what that state is like in ordinary terms, and Buddhist schools have explained it in different ways. Theravada teachers stress the ending of suffering. Many Mahayana traditions add paths such as rebirth in the Pure Land of the Buddha Amitabha.

Buddhist funerals reflect these teachings. Monks chant texts on impermanence, and families make offerings and gifts in the name of the dead to transfer merit to them. In Tibetan Buddhism, the Bardo teachings describe a passage of up to forty-nine days between death and rebirth. Many East Asian families hold memorial rites every seven days through the forty-ninth day. The verse below, from Max Müller's translation of the Dhammapada, is often recalled at such times.

words.d: the Buddhist teaching of non-self: there is no permanent, unchanging soul
in Buddhism, the blowing out of craving and the end of rebirth and suffering
in Buddhism, the good results of wholesome actions, which can be dedicated to others, including the dead

look.title: All Created Things Perish
look.text: 'All created things perish,' he who knows and sees this becomes passive in pain; this is the way that leads to purity.
look.cite: Dhammapada, verse 277, translated by F. Max Müller, Sacred Books of the East, vol. 10 (1881)
look.prompt: Müller's older English says passive in pain; many modern translators say the person grows weary of suffering or turns away from it. How could knowing that all things perish help a grieving person, according to this verse?

check.q: What does the Buddhist teaching of anatta deny?
choices: That karma has results
That suffering exists
That there is a permanent, unchanging soul
That the Buddha taught at all
check.why: Anatta, non-self, denies a permanent soul; a person is a changing stream of body and mind.

check.q: Which image explains Buddhist rebirth in the Questions of King Milinda?
choices: A soul changing clothes
A seed sleeping in the dust
A drop returning to the ocean
A lamp lit from another lamp
check.why: The Questions of King Milinda uses a flame passed from lamp to lamp, neither the same nor different.

check.q: What does nirvana literally mean?
choices: Blowing out, as a flame goes out
Rising again, as the sun rises
Crossing a river
Returning home
check.why: Nirvana means blowing out; craving, the fuel of rebirth, is extinguished.

lessons.title: Jainism and Sikhism: Two Paths to Release
lessons.mainIdea: Jains teach that the soul frees itself from karmic matter through strict nonviolence, while Sikhs teach that liberation comes through God's grace and remembering God's name.
reading: Jainism, the tradition taught by Mahavira in the sixth or fifth century BCE, has the most physical picture of karma in Indian religion. Jains hold that every living being has a *jiva*, an eternal soul, by nature pure and all-knowing. Karma, in Jain teaching, is a fine kind of matter that sticks to the soul through passions such as anger, greed and pride and through harmful action. Weighed down by it, the jiva is reborn again and again.

Liberation comes by stopping new karma and burning off the old. That is why Jains practice ahimsa, nonviolence, with such care, avoiding harm even to insects, and why they value fasting and meditation. A soul entirely freed of karma rises to the top of the universe and dwells there in endless knowledge and bliss. Jains call such liberated souls siddhas. Near the end of life, some devout Jains take a vow of *sallekhana*, gradually giving up food with the approval of their community and teachers. Jains describe it as a peaceful, conscious death, and its practice has been debated in Indian courts.

Sikhism, founded by Guru Nanak (1469–1539), also teaches rebirth driven by karma. But in Sikh teaching, karma is not the last word; God's grace is. Liberation, called *mukti*, comes when a person, by God's grace, remembers the divine Name, lives truthfully and serves others. The self then merges with God, as Sikhs describe it, like water joining water. Sikhs stress that mukti can be experienced in this life, not only after death.

Sikh funerals reflect this. The body is usually cremated, the evening hymn Kirtan Sohila is recited, and the ashes are placed in running water. The family often arranges a complete reading of the Guru Granth Sahib over the following days. Sikh teaching discourages loud wailing, since death is understood as the will of God and a return to God. Both Jains and Sikhs, then, share samsara and karma with Hindus and Buddhists but draw very different maps of the way out.

words.d: in Jainism, the eternal soul present in every living being
a Jain vow near the end of life of gradually giving up food, undertaken with community approval
in Sikhism, liberation from rebirth through God's grace, bringing union with God

look.title: Two Ways Out of the Cycle
look.text: A Jain nun sweeps the path ahead of her with a soft brush so she will not step on insects, and she eats only before sunset. A Sikh volunteer rises before dawn to recite prayers, then spends the morning cooking in the langar. Both believe in rebirth and karma. Both are working toward release.
look.prompt: Explain what each woman believes she is doing about karma. Which one relies more on her own effort, and which one on grace? Use the terms jiva and mukti.

check.q: How does Jainism describe karma?
choices: As a fine matter that sticks to the soul through passions and harmful acts
As God's decision about each person
As an illusion with no effect
As a festival held after a death
check.why: Jain teaching treats karma as a subtle matter that clings to the jiva and weighs it down.

check.q: In Sikh teaching, what brings mukti?
choices: Strict fasting alone
God's grace, with remembering the Name, truthful living and service
Being born into the right family
Visiting Varanasi at death
check.why: Sikhs teach that liberation comes through God's grace as a person remembers the Name and lives truthfully.

check.q: What do Jains and Sikhs share with Hindus and Buddhists?
choices: Belief in a single judgment day
Burial facing Mecca
Belief in samsara and karma
The practice of sallekhana
check.why: All four traditions teach rebirth shaped by karma, though they describe release in different ways.

lessons.title: The Ancestors Remain
lessons.mainIdea: In many African and Chinese traditions the dead become ancestors who stay connected to the living, who honor them and ask for their help.
reading: In early April, many Chinese families go to the cemetery for *Qingming*, the Tomb-Sweeping Festival. They clear weeds, repair the grave, set out food and tea, burn incense and paper offerings, and bow. In many homes an altar holds wooden tablets bearing ancestors' names, and families light incense there on important days. Honoring ancestors in this way is older than Confucius, and Confucian teaching made it central to xiao, filial devotion.

*Ancestor veneration* rests on the idea that the dead continue as members of the family. They are remembered, fed and consulted, and in turn they watch over the living. Chinese popular religion also recognizes spirits with no one to care for them. During the Ghost Festival in the seventh lunar month, families make offerings for these neglected dead. Confucius himself was reserved about the spirit world. When asked about death, he answered that one who does not yet understand life can hardly understand death.

Many African traditions hold a similar picture. Among the Yoruba of West Africa, ancestors are honored at family shrines and, in some communities, in Egungun festivals, where masked dancers are understood to embody the returning dead. Libations, pourings of water or drink on the ground, are offered to ancestors in many African societies. The Kenyan scholar John Mbiti described recently departed ancestors as the living-dead: still remembered by name, still part of the household.

In these traditions death does not end a relationship; it changes it. The ancestor's role depends on being remembered, which makes the living responsible for the dead, and the dead for the living. Scholars note that such traditions often focus less on a final judgment than on the ongoing health of the family and community. Many Christians, Muslims and Buddhists in Africa and East Asia also keep forms of ancestor remembrance, blending older practices with their faith in varied ways.

words.d: honoring deceased family members, who are believed to remain connected to and care for the living
the Chinese Tomb-Sweeping Festival in early April, when families tend graves and honor ancestors
a pouring of water or drink as an offering, often to ancestors

look.title: A Table for the Dead
look.text: At a Chinese American family's home in Chicago's Chinatown, a small altar holds photographs of grandparents, a bowl of oranges, three sticks of incense and a cup of tea that is refilled each morning. At a Yoruba family's shrine, a daughter pours water on the ground and speaks her father's name before asking for his blessing on her new job.
look.prompt: What do both families seem to believe about the dead? How is this different from a view in which the dead go far away to be judged?

check.q: What do Chinese families do at Qingming?
choices: Fast for thirty days
Scatter ashes in a holy river
Read the Guru Granth Sahib in full
Clean graves and offer food, incense and bows to ancestors
check.why: Qingming is the Tomb-Sweeping Festival, when families tend graves and honor their ancestors.

check.q: What did John Mbiti mean by the living-dead?
choices: Recently departed ancestors still remembered by name and part of the household
People who have reached nirvana
Souls waiting in Sheol
Spirits punished in hell
check.why: Mbiti used the term for ancestors who are still remembered and treated as members of the family.

check.q: How did Confucius answer a question about death?
choices: He described heaven in detail
He said one who does not understand life can hardly understand death
He said the soul is reborn
He refused to honor ancestors
check.why: In the Analects, Confucius turns the question back to life, saying one must first understand life.

lessons.title: Job and the Whirlwind
lessons.mainIdea: The Book of Job rejects the idea that suffering is always punishment, and God's answer from the whirlwind points to the limits of human understanding.
reading: The Book of Job opens with a man who is blameless and upright. In a single day he loses his herds, his servants and his ten children. Then his body breaks out in sores. His first response, quoted below, is famous. But then Job sits in the ashes for seven days in silence with three friends, and when he finally speaks, he curses the day he was born. The book that follows is one of the most searching treatments of suffering in world literature.

Job's friends offer the standard explanation. God is just, they say, so suffering must be punishment for sin; Job should confess and be restored. Job insists he has done nothing to deserve this and demands a hearing with God. The book takes Job's side against the friends. At the end, God says that the friends have not spoken rightly, as Job has. The question of how a good and powerful God can allow suffering is called *theodicy*, and Job refuses the easy answer.

When God finally answers, it is from a *whirlwind*, and not with an explanation. Instead God asks Job a long series of questions. Where were you when I laid the foundations of the earth? Can you command the morning, or feed the lion? The speech paints the vastness of creation, far beyond human understanding. Job answers that he has spoken of things too wonderful for him. His fortunes are then restored.

Readers have never agreed on what the ending means. Some Jewish and Christian readers find in it trust: suffering is real, but the world's order is beyond human sight. Others note that Job is never told why he suffered, and they take the book as permission to protest to God. Jewish thinkers after the Holocaust returned to Job for exactly that reason. What most readers agree on is that Job refuses to blame the victim.

words.d: an attempt to explain how a good and all-powerful God can allow evil and suffering
the storm from which God speaks to Job at the end of the Book of Job
a prayer or poem of grief and complaint addressed to God

look.title: The LORD Gave
look.text: And said, Naked came I out of my mother's womb, and naked shall I return thither: the LORD gave, and the LORD hath taken away; blessed be the name of the LORD.
look.prompt: These are Job's first words after losing everything, but by chapter 3 he is cursing the day he was born and uttering a lament. Why might the book include both responses? What does that say about grief?

check.q: What explanation for suffering do Job's friends give?
choices: Suffering is an illusion
Suffering is caused by craving
Suffering must be punishment for sin
Suffering comes from the ancestors
check.why: Job's friends argue that because God is just, Job must have sinned; the book rejects this answer.

check.q: How does God answer Job from the whirlwind?
choices: With a list of Job's sins
With a promise of rebirth
With a law code
With questions about the vastness of creation
check.why: God answers with questions such as where Job was when the earth was founded, not with a direct explanation.

check.q: What is theodicy?
choices: An attempt to explain how a good, powerful God can allow suffering
A Jewish mourning rite
A book of the Qur'an
The Buddhist first truth
check.why: Theodicy is the effort to reconcile God's goodness and power with the existence of suffering.

lessons.title: The Cross and the Test
lessons.mainIdea: Christians believe God entered suffering in Jesus on the cross, while the Qur'an teaches that hardship is a test met with patience and trust in God.
reading: Christianity places a symbol of suffering at its center: the *cross*, on which, the Gospels say, Jesus was executed by Roman authorities. Christians believe that in Jesus God did not stand apart from human pain but entered it. The Gospels record him weeping at a friend's tomb and crying out from the cross in the words of Psalm 22, My God, my God, why hast thou forsaken me? Many Christians take comfort in the belief that God knows suffering from the inside.

Christians also read suffering in the light of the resurrection. Paul writes that the sufferings of this present time are not worth comparing with the glory to come (Romans 8:18). The Book of Revelation ends with a vision, quoted below, of a world in which God wipes away every tear. Christians differ on why suffering exists at all. Some stress human free will; others, God's mystery. Many say that the cross does not explain suffering but shows God sharing it.

The Qur'an speaks of suffering as a *test*. It says God created death and life to test which people are best in deed (67:2). It tells believers that they will be tested with fear, hunger and loss of wealth, lives and crops. Then it gives good news to the patient, who say when disaster strikes: we belong to God, and to God we return (2:155–156). Muslims around the world say those words, in Arabic, on hearing of a death.

The virtue asked of the believer is *sabr*, patience, steadfast endurance with trust in God. The Qur'an also says that God does not burden any soul beyond what it can bear (2:286). Muslims do not read hardship as a sign that God has abandoned a person; the prophets, according to a well-known hadith, were tested most of all. In comparison, Christianity and Islam agree that suffering is not meaningless and not the last word. They differ on whether God suffers: Christians say God did so in Christ, while Islamic teaching holds that God is beyond all suffering.

words.d: the Roman instrument of execution on which Christians believe Jesus died; the central Christian symbol
in the Qur'an, a trial of hardship or ease through which God shows a person's faith and deeds
Arabic for patience; steadfast endurance with trust in God

lessons.title: The First Truth and Karma
lessons.mainIdea: Buddhism begins by naming suffering as a fact of life, and karma explains much suffering in Indian traditions, though teachers warn against using it to blame the suffering.
reading: A young mother named Kisa Gotami, according to a Buddhist story, carried her dead child from house to house, begging for medicine. At last she came to the Buddha. He told her to bring a mustard seed from a household where no one had ever died. She went door to door. Every family had lost someone. By evening she understood that death comes to all. She laid her child to rest and became a nun.

The story illustrates the Buddha's *First Noble Truth*: life as ordinarily lived involves dukkha, suffering or unsatisfactoriness. Birth, aging, sickness and death are dukkha; so is being separated from what one loves. The Buddha did not ask why a creator would allow this, because Buddhism does not teach a creator God. Instead the Second Truth names suffering's cause, craving, and the Third and Fourth teach that it can end and how.

In Hindu, Buddhist and Jain thought, karma explains why suffering falls where it does. Actions have results, and some results ripen in later lives. That can make suffering seem less random: it has a cause, even when the cause cannot be seen. Hindu teachers add that suffering met with patience and devotion can purify the soul. For many believers the idea brings comfort, because in this view the universe is not unjust.

Teachers in all three traditions also warn against misusing karma. In one Buddhist sutta, the Buddha tells a questioner that not every painful feeling comes from past karma. Some come from bodily illness, the change of seasons, careless living or harm done by others. Modern Hindu and Buddhist teachers, and reformers who fought caste discrimination, have argued that karma must never be used to blame the poor or the sick or to excuse cruelty. The compassionate response, all three traditions teach, is to help. Here karma and Job meet: both warn against blaming the one who suffers.

words.d: the Buddha's teaching that ordinary life involves dukkha, suffering or unsatisfactoriness
Pali for suffering, stress or unsatisfactoriness
action and its consequences, which in Indian traditions shape this life and future lives

look.title: The Mustard Seed

lessons.title: Mourning Practices Compared
lessons.mainIdea: Each tradition gives mourners a structure of time, words and actions, and those structures reflect what it believes about death.
reading: In Jewish tradition, burial comes quickly, usually within a day or two. Mourners make a small tear in their clothing, called *kriah*, and after the funeral they sit *shiva*, seven days of mourning at home. Friends visit, bring food and join in prayer, and mirrors are often covered. The mourner's Kaddish, a prayer praising God that never mentions death, is recited for eleven months for a parent. Each year, on the anniversary of the death, families light a candle for the *yahrzeit*.

Christian practice varies widely. Roman Catholics often hold a wake, a funeral Mass and a burial, and they pray for the dead in the months afterward. The Catholic Church has permitted cremation since 1963, though it asks that ashes be kept in a sacred place rather than scattered. Protestant funerals often center on Scripture, hymns and memories of the person. Orthodox Christians hold memorial services on the third, ninth and fortieth days after death.

Muslims bury the dead quickly after washing and shrouding the body, and the community joins in a funeral prayer. The general period of mourning is three days, while a widow observes a longer waiting period of four months and ten days. Hindus usually cremate, and the family observes a period of impurity and rites that often lasts about thirteen days. Sikhs cremate and read the Guru Granth Sahib. In many East Asian Buddhist traditions, rites continue every seven days until the forty-ninth.

Set side by side, the practices share a pattern. They give mourners a first intense period, a longer season, and a yearly remembrance. They bring the community to the mourner's door. And each reflects a belief. Quick burial facing Mecca points to resurrection and judgment. Cremation points to a soul that has moved on. The Kaddish points to God's greatness in the face of loss. Forty-nine days points to a passage toward rebirth.

words.d: the seven days of mourning at home observed by Jewish families after a burial
the Jewish practice of tearing one's garment as a sign of grief
the yearly anniversary of a death in Jewish tradition, marked by lighting a candle

lessons.title: Secular and Humanist Answers
lessons.mainIdea: Secular thinkers and humanists generally hold that death is the end of the person and that meaning is found in this life, in love, memory and the good one does.
reading: Nearly three in ten American adults now describe themselves as having no religion, and many of them, though not all, believe that death is simply the end of the person. That view is old. The Greek philosopher Epicurus, around 300 BCE, argued that death should not be feared, because where death is, we are not, and where we are, death is not. A person who no longer exists, he reasoned, cannot suffer. He wanted his students to live calmly and well.

Modern *humanism* builds on this. Humanists hold that people can live meaningful, ethical lives without belief in God or an afterlife. They say meaning is not given from outside but made, in relationships, work, creativity and service. A humanist funeral, often led by a trained celebrant, centers on the life of the person who died. There are stories, music and tributes, and no prayers for the soul. Humanists speak of the dead living on in memory and in the difference they made.

On suffering, secular thinkers do not need a theodicy, since they do not believe in a God whose goodness must be defended. Some argue that the amount of suffering in the world is itself a reason to doubt such a God. This is the *problem of evil*, an argument often traced back to Epicurus. Others simply treat suffering as part of nature, to be reduced through medicine, science and justice, and borne with courage when it cannot be.

The secular view shares ground with religious ones. Like Buddhists, many secular thinkers stress accepting impermanence. Like Jews, many emphasize this life over speculation about the next. Like everyone, they grieve, gather and remember. What differs is the claim underneath: that nothing of the person continues beyond memory and influence. Religious believers, in turn, often say that without a hope beyond death some suffering cannot be answered. A fair comparison lets each side state its answer in full.

words.d: a nonreligious outlook holding that people can live meaningful, ethical lives through reason and compassion, without God
the argument that the existence of great suffering is hard to reconcile with a good, all-powerful God
not connected with religion or religious belief
